Credential Type
Tags: programs
Short Description: Identifies the type of academic credential awarded for a program. (Degree, Major, Minor, Certificate)
Credential Type

The degree is the academic credential awarded by the University upon successful completion of an approved program of study and its associated requirements. Degrees may include bachelor's, master's, and doctoral degrees.
The major is the primary field of study within a degree program, consisting of a defined set of courses and requirements that students must complete.
University Manual 8.20.40 Major Fields of Study. An undergraduate student’s concentrated field of study in a degree-granting college shall be the student’s “major”; Fannon Institute students may have a “preferred major.” The major field of study for graduate students shall be the student’s “program.”

Undergraduate programs are required to have a minimum or 120 credits, and a maximum of 148 (UM 8.21.10)
Undergraduate programs shall include at least 6 credits of free electives (UM 8.21.10)
General Education requirements shall apply to all undergraduate programs (UM 8.21.11)
A cumulative average of at least 2.00 is required to graduate from all undergraduate degrees. (UM 8.22.10)
Master’s degree programs with thesis require a minimum of 30 credits. 18 must be from content-based courses, 6 must be thesis courses. (GSM 7.44.1)
Master’s degree programs without thesis require a minimum of 30 credits. (GSM 7.45.1)
Doctoral students must complete a Program of Study with a minimum of 64 credit hours beyond the undergraduate degree (GSM 7.54) (See GSM sections 7.54 and 7.21)
In Kuali, the term program refers to all credential types; Degrees, majors, minors, and certificates. In the Manual, program refers to a graduate student’s major field of study.

A secondary concentration of undergraduate courses that provides students with a defined area of study outside their major. A minor generally requires 18 or more credits and is listed on the student’s permanent academic record after graduation.
University Manual 8.20.50 Minor Fields of Study. Undergraduate Students may declare a “minor” field of study. A minor is a secondary concentration of courses.

18 or more credits of related studies offered by one or more departments or programs and sponsored by a faculty member. (UM 8.20.50)
At least 12 credits at the 200-level or above ( UM 8.20.51)
At least 8 credits must be earned at URI (UM 8.20.51)
Minimum GPA average of 2.0 must be earned in the minor’s required courses (UM 8.20.51)
A maximum of two courses can apply to both the major and minor field of study (UM 8.20.52)
An approved course of study designed to further knowledge in a field of interest, provide specialized training, and/or enhance professional skills.

Undergraduate certificates generally require 15-21 credits of coursework (UM 8.20.70)
Undergraduate certificates are available to degree seeking and certificate-only seeking undergraduate students (UM 8.20.70)
Undergraduate certificate courses may not be pass/fail (UM 8.20.71)
Graduate certificates require 12 credits minimum, 16 credits maximum. (GSM Appendix J.1.1)
Post-master’s graduate certificates require 12 credits minimum, 18 credits maximum. (GSM Appendix J.1.1)

Specialization Description
Tags: specializations
Short Description: The University Catalog description of a program specialization, including its specialization-specific curriculum and any additional requirements for completion.
Specialization Description
The University Catalog description of the requirements for completing a specialization within an academic program, including the specialization-specific courses and credits required in addition to the program’s core requirements, as well as any additional specialization-specific requirements.

Descriptive overview: A brief paragraph explaining the purpose and significance of the specialization.
Course Requirements
Important: Do not include program requirements in the specialization description.
Only include the requirements of the specialization in the specialization description, and exclude the core requirements to the program. The specialization
A specialization is an addition to the academic program, not a second listing of the program’s requirements. Students complete the requirements of the program and, where applicable, the additional requirements of their chosen specialization. The specialization description should therefore include only the requirements that are specific to that specialization.
Repeating the program requirements within the specialization could imply that students must complete those requirements again as part of the specialization. Keeping program-wide requirements in the program description and specialization-specific requirements in the specialization description makes it clear which requirements apply to the program as a whole and which are additional requirements for the specialization.
(For ABMs only) Courses that are able to be double-counted

A minimum GPA average of 2.00 must be earned in the specialization courses (UM 8.20.61)
Half of the credits required for the specialization must be earned at URI (UM 8.20.61)
A maximum of one third of the total credits required for a master’s program may be double counted for an ABM program. (UM 8.30.19)

Track Your Proposal
Track Your Proposal
Quick Links
Submitting a curricular proposal in Kuali begins a structured, multi-level review process, and we know you’re eager to know when your item will be reviewed and approved. While timelines vary across colleges, this guide will help you understand where your proposal is in the process and when to expect its full approval.

For those who already know how the process works, but simply need directions on where to find the status:
Open the proposal in Kuali
Expand the workflow status

All curricular proposals move through multiple levels of review. While this can vary slightly, most proposals follow this sequence:
Department-level review(s)
College Curriculum Committee
College Dean
Faculty Senate Curriculum Committees (Graduate Council, Curriculum & Standards, General Education)
Faculty Senate (courses are fully approved at this level)
University President (program modifications and new certificates, minors, and specializations are approved at this level)
Board of Trustees (new major and degree programs are approved at this level)
Each step depends on the successful approval at the previous level.
Check out The Approval Process for a flowchart and more detailed explanation of the approval process.

All who have access to Kuali have the ability to check on the status of every proposal currently under review. To find the current workflow status:
Open the proposal in Kuali.
Access it from your dashboard if you are the proposer, or
Search for it in the Proposals section, and use filters to refine results
Review the workflow status. At the top of the proposal page, the workflow status shows:
The current stage of approval
The users in the role of approving that step
Expand for full details. Clik the expand option to the right of “Workflow Status” to view:
The completed approval steps, and
The remaining steps before final approval.

Department, college, and Faculty Senate committees each have deadlines for including proposals on their meeting agendas. Faculty should consult with their department or college curriculum committees for specific deadlines at those levels of approval.
Each summer, submission deadlines are set for college deans to help ensure proposals are approved by the Faculty Senate on a predictable timeline.

Curriculum proposals must receive all required approvals by specific deadlines to take effect for their intended term. Deadlines vary by proposal type and may be influenced by registration dates, implementation requirements, and additional University approvals.

Many proposals require revisions during the review process. The following meeting results can impact your approval timeline:
Tabled: The committee needs additional information before making a decision. Once the requested information is provided, the proposal will be reviewed again at the next meeting.
Contingently Approved: The proposal is approved pending minor revisions or clarifications. No additional committee review is required. Once the conditions are met, the proposal will move to the next step.
Sent Back: The proposal requires substantial revisions. It must be updated and resubmitted, at which point it will re-enter the workflow from the beginning.

Proposal statuses can be tracked by logging into Kuali and expanding the workflow, or by searching for items that have been fully approved by the college in the proposal tracker.
2026-2027 Proposal Tracker
Please note: The proposal tracker is updated manually by the Faculty Senate Office and is not automated. While every effort is made to ensure accuracy, occasional errors may occur and are typically corrected after each Faculty Senate meeting. For the most up-to-date status, please check Kuali.

By the Monday prior to each monthly Faculty Senate meeting, the Faculty Senate Office distributes the Senate agenda to all faculty.
This agenda includes reports from the Graduate Council, Curriculum & Standards Committee, and General Education Committee, which are voted on during the meeting.
If your proposal has been approved by a committee but does not appear on the agenda, please contact the committee chair or the Faculty Senate Office. Reports are prepared manually, and with a high volume of proposals each month, occasional errors may occur. These are typically resolved quickly.

The integration between Kuali and PeopleSoft is not immediate, can take several days, and requires review by Enrollment Services to ensure all information migrated accurately. Please allow up to two weeks after the Senate Meeting for new courses and course modifications to appear in eCampus.

Once curriculum committee reports are approved by the Faculty Senate, they are converted into Bills. Bills are signed by the Faculty Senate President and forwarded to the University President for review and signature. Once the University President signs & approves, the Bills are returned to the Faculty Senate Office and the proposals are approved in Kuali.
Special Case: New Majors and New Degree Programs
After University President approval, these proposals are forwarded to the Board of Trustees. Once the Faculty Senate Office confirms Board approval, the new major or degree is fully approved in Kuali.

Kuali Basics
Kuali Basics
Quick Links

Kuali Curriculum Management (CM) is URI’s system for managing university curriculum and the curriculum approval process. It uses electronic forms and workflow to route course, program, and specialization proposals through the appropriate levels of review and approval.

Kuali serves as the central source for approved curriculum information:
Kuali CM — Manages curriculum proposals and the approval workflow.
Academic Catalog — Pulls approved course, program, and specialization information from Kuali.
eCampus — Receives approved course information from Kuali for implementation in future terms.

Information entered into Kuali can flow directly into the official academic catalog and eCampus. Proposals should therefore be clear, accurate, and unambiguous, as the information entered during the proposal process becomes part of the University’s official curriculum.
Access to Kuali CM is limited to faculty, Deans, and select administrators and staff. Only faculty members may submit curriculum proposals.

Faculty members automatically have access to Kuali CM, as faculty are the users authorized to submit curricular proposals. If this is your first time accessing Kuali CM, sign in using your URI Microsoft 365 account.

Access to Kuali CM is also available to deans and select administrators or staff. In specific cases, other non-faculty users may request access.
Use the Kuali Access Package to request access using your URI SSO. After selecting Continue, you will be asked to provide your job or position title and a business justification for needing access. Once your request has been reviewed, you will be notified whether access has been granted.

Sign in to your Microsoft 365 Apps using your URI SSO.
Select Kuali Course Management from your application collection.
Alternatively, use the direct link to Kuali CM and bookmark it for future access.
Once logged in, select the Curriculum tile. This is where you can view current courses, programs, and specializations and, for authorized users, create proposals for new or modified curriculum.
When you enter Curriculum Management, the Dashboard serves as your homepage. It provides quick access to your proposals and items requiring your action.

My Proposals allows you to:
Continue working on Drafts you have started but not yet submitted.
View submitted proposals and their current workflow status.
Access proposals directly from the Dashboard.
Any proposals you begin but have not yet submitted will appear as Drafts. From this section, you can continue editing or delete a draft.
Select View All to see your complete list of proposals. The list can be filtered, downloaded, and printed.

My Action List displays your ten most recent items requiring action. These may include proposals that require you to:
Review and approve
Acknowledge
Edit and return to the workflow after being sent back by a reviewing committee
Use the navigation bar on the left side of the screen to access courses, programs, specializations, and proposals, including drafts, proposals under review, and approved records.

Use the search bar at the top of the Courses, Programs, Specializations, or Proposals pages to locate specific records. Use the filters on the right side of the page to narrow your results.
Status: Select Active when searching for current curricular items. Retired and Inactive statuses are not consistently used in Kuali CM.
Groups: Use Groups to locate curricular records associated with a specific department or college.

Kuali uses colored bars to indicate which version of a curricular record you are viewing.
🟢 Current Version — The version currently in effect. For most records, the earliest version available in Kuali is Fall 2022, when URI began using Kuali. Earlier historical versions are available in eCampus.
⚪ Past Version — An earlier version of the record, including inactive records.
🟣 Future Version — A version scheduled to become active in a future term.
↕️ Use the arrows next to the term dates to expand the record history and select an earlier or future version.

The status indicators below apply only when you are viewing a proposal and not the curricular record itself. The colored bar at the top of a proposal indicates where the proposal is in the curriculum approval workflow.
🟡 Draft — A new proposal or proposed change that has been created but not yet submitted to the workflow. Drafts can be edited or deleted.
🔵 Under Review — A proposal that has been submitted to the workflow and is currently moving through the approval process.
⚫ Denied — A proposal that has been denied during the review process. Denied proposals cannot be edited or resubmitted.
🟢 Approved — A proposal that has completed the required approval process and has been approved.
Tip: When viewing an approved proposal, you can switch to the current curricular record by selecting “View Active Course (Program / Specialization).”

Method of Instruction
Tags: courses
Short Description: The instructional delivery method. Also known as "class component.”
Method of Instruction
Provided below is the complete list of approved methods of instruction, as proposed in FSEC Report #2024-2025-03 and subsequently approved by the Faculty Senate through Bill #24-25-12 on January 23, 2025.
A course in which the primary method is presentation and students are expected to participate in a variety of ways, such as small-group discussions, questions and answers, writing-exercises, etc.
Applied course work, generally involving experimentation or observation, typically using special equipment (including computers and specialized software).
Separate sections of a lecture course regularly scheduled for discussion.
Supervised work with an emphasis on performance and creativity in which faculty instruct, assist, and critique.
Course offered to a small group (usually no more than 20 students) where participants actively exchange ideas and findings based on readings or research.

One-on-one instruction in which the student enters into an agreement with the instructor that defines the focus of inquiry and nature of activities. Includes tutorials, directed readings, special projects.
Structured experiences where the primary aim is to connect theory with practice. Includes clinics, internships, externships, student teaching, field experiences. May include regular class meetings.
Similar to a seminar, with emphasis on applied rather than theoretical learning, but not offered for degree-program credit.
